intro: What each finished feature does, who can use it and how, with screenshots of the real screens. Screenshots are re-taken from the running demo by `npm run docs:shots` (frontend), so they follow the UI; the page is rebuilt by `node tools/build-feature-docs.mjs`. See .claude/skills/feature-docs/SKILL.md.

features.title: Personal access tokens (API tokens for scripts and MCP)
features.summary: Anyone can create long-lived tokens on their profile so a script or an AI assistant (an MCP client) can work as them without their password. Each token works in one place, as at most the role chosen for it, and never more than its owner may do now. Expiry is chosen per token: 7, 30, 90 or 365 days, a custom number of days, or none.
who: Every signed-in person, in every role
Partner roles: Partner admin, Partner viewer

flow.title: Follow one token from creation to every call
flow.intro: The boxes are the parts a token passes through; the pill is the token or the request carrying it. Pick a situation.

nodes.label: Security filter
nodes.sub: Checks every call that carries fsp_…

nodes.label: Token table
nodes.sub: Only a fingerprint, scope, role, expiry

steps.say: You name the token, choose where it works, the most it may do, and when it expires.
The server makes a random token and shows it to you once. Copy it now.
steps.tech: 32 random bytes, Base64, prefixed `fsp_`.

steps.say: Only a fingerprint is saved, never the token itself. Even a database leak gives nobody a usable token.
steps.tech: SHA-256 of the token, plus scope, role ceiling and expiry.

steps.say: Your script sends the token with its request.
The filter fingerprints the token and finds its row: not revoked, not expired.
steps.tech: One indexed lookup by fingerprint.

steps.say: It checks that you still belong to that organization, and what your role allows today.
steps.tech: Permissions = token role AND your current role.

steps.say: It makes a short sign-in token for this call only, with that organization and the narrowed role.
steps.tech: ES256-signed JWT, kept in memory.

steps.say: The call continues like any signed-in call: the organization in the path must match.
The database itself only shows this project's rows.
An owner lowers your role from Admin to Analyst.
Your script calls again with a token made as Admin.
The next call already uses the lower role: a token never does more than you may do now.
steps.tech: The narrowing is computed on every call, not when the token was made.

steps.say: Editing is refused; reading still works.
You revoke the token on the API Tokens tab.
The row is marked revoked and this server forgets its cached answer at once.
steps.tech: `revoked_at` set; other servers follow within 30 seconds.

steps.say: The script tries again with the old token.
Refused. The failure is logged by address, but never blocks other, valid tokens.
A token made for one organization is sent to the platform API or to the password endpoint.
Refused: organization tokens only reach /api/orgs/…, platform tokens only /api/platform/…, and no token can change passwords or tokens.
steps.tech: A web rule per token scope.

steps: Open your profile (your name, top right) and choose the API Tokens tab.
Give the token a name that says what uses it, e.g. "Claude desktop (read-only)".
Choose where it works: one of your organizations, or Platform administration (platform administrators only).
Choose the most it may do. Only your own role and lower ones are offered; Read-only is the default.
Choose when it expires, or No expiry.
Create it and copy the token straight away: it starts with fsp_ and is shown only once.
Use it as the header Authorization: Bearer fsp_… in the script or MCP client. Revoke it on the same tab when it is no longer needed.
rules: Only a SHA-256 fingerprint of the token is stored; the token itself is shown once.
Every call is checked again: a revoked or expired token, a removed membership or a lowered role takes effect at once.
A token never does more than the role chosen for it or the owner's current role (the permissions are the intersection).
Organization tokens reach only that organization's API (/api/orgs/{org}/…; partners also /api/partners/{partner}/…). Platform tokens reach only /api/platform/…. All can read GET /api/auth/me.
Tokens can't change passwords or create, list or revoke tokens.

Tokens are 256-bit random values, so they can't be guessed. Bad tokens are logged per client address for monitoring, but never block valid tokens (one old script retrying a revoked token must not lock out a whole office).
Creating and revoking tokens is recorded in the organization's (or platform's) audit trail.
There is no FAST Studio MCP server yet: MCP clients need a server that calls this API with the token.
api: POST /api/auth/personal-tokens {name, org (id, slug or "platform"), role, expiresInDays (null = no expiry)}
Any allowed API call with Authorization: Bearer fsp_…

screenshots.caption: The API Tokens tab: name, where it works, the most it may do (your role or lower) and the expiry.
Right after creating: the token is shown once to copy (hidden in this picture). Here it was made with No expiry.
A platform administrator can make platform-scope tokens for /api/platform/….
Partner members choose partner roles (Partner admin or Read-only partner viewer) for the partner API.

features.cleanup: fetch('/api/auth/personal-tokens').then(r => r.json()).then(list => Promise.all(list.filter(t => t.name.startsWith('Docs:')).map(t => fetch('/api/auth/personal-tokens/' + t.id, { method: 'DELETE', headers: { 'X-XSRF-TOKEN': decodeURIComponent((document.cookie.match(/XSRF-TOKEN=([^;]+)/) || [])[1] || '') } }))))
howItWorks: Creating: 32 random bytes become the token (fsp_ + Base64). Only its SHA-256 fingerprint, the scope (organization, or none for platform), the role ceiling and the expiry are saved; the token itself is returned once.

Using: when a request carries Authorization: Bearer fsp_…, the security filter fingerprints it, finds the row, checks it is neither revoked nor expired and that the owner still belongs to that organization (or is still a platform administrator).

It then mints an ordinary 10-minute signed sign-in token (JWT) in memory, with only that organization and the narrowed role, and the request continues exactly like a normal signed-in call: organization-in-path check, database membership check and row-level security all apply.

Narrowing: permissions = what the chosen role allows AND what the owner's current role (including custom roles) allows; the role is the lower of the two. A demotion or removal therefore applies to the very next call.

Fencing: a web rule lets organization tokens reach only /api/orgs/… (partners also /api/partners/…), platform tokens only /api/platform/…, and every token GET /api/auth/me. Account endpoints (password, tokens) are never reachable with a token.
Revoking sets revoked_at; the server forgets its cached "still valid" answer at once.
optimizations: Lookup is one probe on a unique index (token_hash); the secret is never compared character by character, so there is no timing leak.
last_used_at is written at most once a minute per token, so a busy script doesn't turn every read into a database write.
The "is this token still valid" check on the minted sign-in token is cached for 30 seconds per server, like the existing sign-in version check.
Nothing is stored per call: no sessions, no saved access tokens. Servers stay stateless and interchangeable.
The profile tab loads one list request only when it is opened (the screen code itself is downloaded on demand).
Each person may keep at most 25 active tokens, which keeps the table and the list small.
scale: Per call the exchange costs about four small indexed queries and one ES256 signature (well under a millisecond of CPU). That is comfortable for scripts and AI assistants making tens to hundreds of calls a second per server.
Any number of servers can serve tokens: all state is in PostgreSQL and nothing is tied to one server.
Bad tokens cost one indexed lookup and are logged per client address in the shared database; a 256-bit token can't be guessed, so valid tokens are never blocked by an address's failures.

Known ceiling: a single token driving thousands of calls a second pays the exchange on every call. Upgrade path: cache the minted sign-in token per token fingerprint for its 10-minute life, keyed on the owner's token version and cleared on revoke.
Revocation is immediate on the server that handled it and within 30 seconds on other servers (the shared validity cache). Use "sign out everywhere" or a role change for an instant stop everywhere.

features.title: Sign-in protection and security headers
features.summary: Limits on guessing passwords, reset emails and partner credentials, shared by every server; outbound address checks on ad servers and remote media including redirects; ad-tag URLs encrypted at rest; browser security headers. Nothing to click: it works in the background.

flow.title: See how guessing and bad addresses are stopped
flow.intro: The boxes are the parts that protect sign-in and outbound calls; the pill is one attempt or request. Pick a situation.

nodes.label: Visitor
nodes.sub: Signs in or asks for a reset

nodes.label: Any server
nodes.sub: Every server shares the same limits

nodes.label: Attempt log (auth_attempt)
nodes.sub: Counts per account and per address

steps.say: Someone signs in with an email and password.
The server counts recent failures for that account and that address. Both are under the limit.
steps.tech: Two indexed counts in the shared database.

steps.say: Only then is the password checked.
Correct: the account's failure count is cleared and the person is in.
Someone tries wrong passwords for one account.
Each failure adds a row for that account (stored as a hash, not the email).
steps.tech: Bucket `login-email:<hash>`.

steps.say: The sixth try is refused with "Too many attempts" before the password is even checked. It waits a few minutes.
An attacker spreads guesses across several servers behind the load balancer.
All servers count in the same database table, so spreading out doesn't help.
steps.tech: Limits survive restarts too.

steps.say: From one address, 20 failures in 15 minutes and the address waits, whichever server it reaches.
An ad break needs ads from an external ad server.
The ad tag address is stored encrypted; it is opened only now.
steps.tech: AES-256-GCM.

steps.say: The address is resolved: it must be a public internet host, not the platform's own network.
steps.tech: Private, loopback, link-local and carrier-grade NAT ranges are refused.

steps.say: Public, so the call is made. Each redirect hop is checked the same way.
An ad server answers with a redirect pointing at an internal address.
The guard checks the new hop before following it and refuses: no request reaches the internal network.
steps.tech: Redirects are followed one hop at a time by hand. Not yet covered: DNS rebinding between check and connect.

steps: After 5 wrong passwords for one account within 5 minutes, that account waits a few minutes ("Too many attempts").
After 20 failed sign-ins from one address within 15 minutes (many accounts), that address waits.
One address can request at most 10 password-reset emails an hour; each account gets at most 3 an hour.
Partner client-credential guessing is limited per address the same way (20 failures per 15 minutes). Bad personal tokens are logged per address but never block valid ones.
rules: Limits are stored in the database (auth_attempt), so they hold across restarts and several servers; emails are stored only as hashes.
Behind a proxy the visitor's address is taken from X-Forwarded-For only when the proxy is on a private network.
Ad-server and remote media addresses must be public http(s) hosts; every redirect hop is checked too.
Ad-tag URLs are encrypted (AES-GCM) in the database; older plaintext rows are encrypted at start-up.
Pages send Content-Security-Policy (only the app's own scripts, no framing), Referrer-Policy and Permissions-Policy.
howItWorks: Each counted event (a wrong password, a reset-email request, a bad partner secret or personal token) adds one row to auth_attempt with a bucket such as login-email:<hash> or login-ip:<address>.

Before the check runs, the server counts that bucket's rows in its time window; at the limit it answers 429 "Too many attempts" without checking the password. A successful sign-in clears the account's bucket.

Outbound addresses (ad servers, VAST wrappers, creative and remote video files) are resolved and refused when they point at a private, loopback, link-local, carrier-grade-NAT or other non-public network. Redirects are followed one hop at a time and each hop is checked again; for remote video the final address is resolved before ffmpeg starts.
Ad-tag URLs are sealed with AES-256-GCM before saving and opened only when an ad waterfall is built; rows saved before encryption are sealed automatically at start-up.
Every page carries a Content-Security-Policy that allows only the app's own scripts and forbids framing, plus Referrer-Policy and Permissions-Policy.
optimizations: One composite index (bucket, created_at) makes every limit check a short index range scan.
Only failures are counted for sign-in, so normal users add no rows; emails are stored as SHA-256 hashes (no personal data in the table).
An hourly job deletes rows older than a day, so the table stays small however long the system runs.
Inside the security filter the token limit uses a non-throwing check, so an over-limit request is a clean 401 instead of an error page.
Redirect checking reuses one HTTP client per source (connection pooling) and stops after 5 hops.
AES-GCM decryption of an ad tag takes microseconds and happens only when the waterfall is read.
scale: A sign-in adds two indexed counts (and two inserts only when it fails). That is tiny next to the deliberate cost of checking a password hash (bcrypt, tens of milliseconds), so the limiter is never the bottleneck.
Limits are shared by every server through PostgreSQL and survive restarts, so scaling out doesn't loosen them.
Behind a load balancer the real visitor address is used (X-Forwarded-For from private-network proxies only), so one busy proxy doesn't lock everyone out and visitors can't fake their address.

Known ceiling: a very large credential-stuffing attack (millions of attempts an hour) would still reach the application and the database. Block such floods earlier with Cloudflare rate limiting or WAF rules in front; this database limiter is the second line.
DNS rebinding between the address check and the actual connection is not yet prevented; the upgrade is an HTTP client that connects only to the checked address.

features.title: Tenant isolation in the database
features.summary: Each customer only ever sees its own data, and the database itself enforces it: even a bug in the application can't read or change another customer's rows. Work that must span customers (background jobs, platform administration) runs through a separate, tightly held database login. Nothing to click: it applies to every screen and API.

flow.title: See how the database keeps customers apart
flow.intro: The boxes are the layers every request passes through; the pill is one request or one database row. Pick a situation.

nodes.label: Row-level security
nodes.sub: Every row compared with the stamp

steps.say: Someone at Aurora opens the Library.
The organization in the path must be in their sign-in token, and they must still be a member.
A database connection is borrowed and stamped with Aurora.
steps.tech: `set_config('app.org_id', …)` on every checkout.

steps.say: The database compares every row with the stamp, on top of the app's own organization filter.
Only Aurora's videos come back.
Imagine a coding mistake: a query without any organization filter.
Row-level security still applies, because the database does it, not the code.
Northwind's rows are simply not there for this connection.
The mistake returns only Aurora's rows. A CI check also catches the missing filter before it ships.
steps.tech: `tools/check-tenant-filters.mjs`.

steps.say: An Aurora user types Northwind's project into the address.
Refused before any data is read: they are not a member. The answer is "not found", so it doesn't even confirm the project exists.
A request stamped with Aurora tries to write a row that belongs to Northwind.
PostgreSQL rejects the row: new rows must match the stamp too.
steps.tech: Policy `with check (fs_tenant_ok(org_id))`.

steps.say: A background job needs to look across projects, such as picking the next video to convert.
It uses its own connection pool with a separate login that the rules trust. A request connection can't switch to it.
steps.tech: Trust is based on `session_user`, which `set role` cannot change.

steps.say: Once it knows which project a job belongs to, it does the actual work as that project only.

steps: Every project API path names the organization (/api/orgs/{organization}/…); platform tenant routes name the tenant (/api/platform/tenants/{tenant}/…).
The sign-in token carries the organization (org) and its tenant (tid); the organization in the path must be one the token lists and the person belongs to, otherwise the answer is 404.
Every database query of a project names that organization, and the database adds its own check on top.
howItWorks: Requests use a database login (faststudio_app_login) that may only see rows of the organization stamped on its connection. It is not the table owner and cannot switch to any other role.

Each borrowed connection is stamped with the current organization (app.org_id); PostgreSQL row-level security policies compare every row's organization with it. An unfiltered "select * from asset" returns only that project's videos, and inserting a row for another organization fails.

Cross-tenant system work (platform administration, media jobs, alert scans, edge publishing, partner client sign-in) gets its connection from a separate pool that logs in as faststudio_system_login. The policies trust that login, identified by session_user, which a request connection cannot become.

Both logins are created and kept up to date after every database migration; their passwords are derived from the server's secrets key, so every server sharing the key uses the same ones and nothing extra is configured.

Every table that carries an organization has a policy; organization and membership (they establish the tenant), personal tokens (they belong to a person) and the platform email outbox are deliberately outside, and a test fails if any other table is missing one.
In the code, every SQL statement on a tenant table also names the organization explicitly (or is marked as deliberate cross-tenant system work); a CI check enforces this.
optimizations: The organization is stamped once per connection checkout with one tiny statement; no per-query overhead in the application.
Policies are simple equality checks on org_id, which the tenant-first indexes serve directly, so row-level security adds no extra table reads.

System work and requests use separate connection pools (10 each per server; the system pool also serves viewer session lookups and platform administration), so a burst of background work can't take every request connection.
scale: All projects share one database, so adding a customer costs one row, not a database. Isolation does not weaken with more customers: every query is filtered by organization in the database itself.
Indexes on large tables lead with org_id, so one project's queries read only its own slice however large other projects grow.

Known ceiling: one PostgreSQL server for all tenants. Upgrade path, in order: connection pooling (PgBouncer), read replicas for reports, then sharding by tenant (e.g. Citus) without changing the application. A dedicated database for one tenant is possible when a contract requires it.
Not measured: behaviour under sustained multi-tenant load.
rules: A request connection that tries "set role" to the system role is refused; "reset role" leaves it as the same restricted login.
The old app.bypass session switch no longer exists; setting it changes nothing.
The configured database user only migrates and must be allowed to create roles (CREATEROLE).

features.title: Durable media processing
features.summary: Converting a video into 5-second segments is a job stored in the database, so it survives restarts and crashes, runs exactly once even with several servers, retries by itself when the problem is temporary, can be cancelled, and one busy project can't hold up the others. Nothing new to click yet: the Library shows the same statuses; the job history is available through the API.
who: Owners, admins and operators (cancel; needs asset editing)

flow.title: Watch a job move through the system
flow.intro: Each box is one part of the system; the moving pill is one video's job and its current state. Pick a situation to see how it behaves, step by step.

nodes.label: You
nodes.sub: Upload, sample, retry or library sync

nodes.label: Job table (media_job)
nodes.sub: The one place that decides who does what

steps.say: You upload a video. In the same save, a job is written for it.
steps.tech: `insert into media_job` in the same database transaction as the asset change: no change without a job, no job without its change.

steps.say: The job waits in the table. Clicking twice or a repeated webhook adds nothing.
steps.tech: A partial unique index allows one active job per video; a second insert is `on conflict do nothing`.

steps.say: A free worker on any server takes it. Only one worker can get it.
steps.tech: `update … where id = (select … for update skip locked limit 1)`. The claim gets fence 1 and a 2-minute lease.

steps.say: ffmpeg converts the video. Every 30 seconds the worker tells the table it is still alive.
steps.tech: Heartbeat: `lease_until = now() + 2 min where id = … and fence = 1`.

steps.say: The result goes into a brand-new folder, so what is on air is never touched halfway.
steps.tech: Folder name `{project}/{video}.{time}`: every run is a new revision.

steps.say: Published in one step: the video switches to the new media and the job is marked done.
steps.tech: One SQL statement updates job and video together, only while the fence is still 1.

steps.say: A video is waiting in the queue.
Worker A on server 1 takes it.
steps.tech: Fence 1, lease until now + 2 minutes.

steps.say: Server 1 dies in the middle of the job. Its heartbeats stop.
steps.tech: Nobody extends `lease_until` any more.

steps.say: Once the lease has run out, the reaper puts the job back in the queue.
steps.tech: `state = 'RUNNING' and lease_until < now()` becomes QUEUED, to try again after 1 minute.

steps.say: Worker B on server 2 takes it over.
steps.tech: Claiming again raises the fence to 2.

steps.say: Published. Nothing was lost, and the job never ran twice at the same time.
Worker A is converting the video.
Worker A freezes for a long time (for example, a stuck machine). Its lease runs out.
The reaper re-queues the job and Worker B takes it, with fence 2.
Worker B publishes its result. The video now plays B's media.
Worker A wakes up and tries to publish its older result.
steps.tech: `… where fence = 1` matches 0 rows: the table holds fence 2.

steps.say: Worker A deletes its own output and stops. The newer media stays on air.
A video is being converted.
You cancel it.
steps.tech: `POST /api/orgs/{org}/assets/{id}/jobs/cancel`. A job still waiting in the queue would be cancelled right away.

steps.say: At its next heartbeat (within 30 seconds) the worker sees the cancel.
steps.tech: The heartbeat returns the job's state.

steps.say: The worker kills ffmpeg.
The half-made output is deleted.
The old media keeps airing. A video that never had media goes back to Draft.
A worker starts a video from the connected library.
The library isn't ready to hand over the original file yet: a temporary problem.
steps.tech: The content source throws `Retryable`; unexpected errors count as temporary too.

steps.say: The job goes back to the queue and waits. The video still shows Processing.
steps.tech: Waits of 1, 5, 25 and 125 minutes between tries.

steps.say: Next time, any free worker takes it again.
This time it works and is published. After 5 failed tries the video shows Failed with the reason. A broken file fails at once, without retrying.
Project A queues 6 videos, then project B queues 1.
Project A's first video starts.
Project A's second video starts. A now runs its maximum of 2 at once.
The next free worker skips project A's waiting videos and takes B's.
steps.tech: The claim skips projects already running `faststudio.media.jobs-per-project` (2) programme jobs. Ads have their own lane.

steps.say: One project's big import can't hold up everyone else.

steps: Create a sample, upload a file, retry a failed video or sync the library: the video shows PROCESSING and a job is queued with that change.
To see what is happening, call GET /api/orgs/{organization}/assets/{video}/jobs: state, attempt, last error and, while waiting for a retry, when it runs next.
To stop it, call POST /api/orgs/{organization}/assets/{video}/jobs/cancel. A video that was already ready keeps its old media on air; a new one goes back to DRAFT.
howItWorks: The job row is written in the same database transaction as the change that needs it, so there is never a change without a job or a job without its change. A second request for the same video does nothing while one is active.
Worker threads on every server ask the database for the next due job; FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED hands each job to exactly one of them.
A running job holds a 2-minute lease that its worker renews every 30 seconds. If the server dies, the lease runs out and the job goes back to the queue within about a minute.

Every claim gets a new fence number. The finished video is published (asset and job in one statement) only if the fence still matches, so a worker that lost its job can never replace newer media; the currently airing media is untouched until then.
Temporary failures (library not ready, address unreachable, unexpected errors) retry after 1, 5, 25 and 125 minutes, then fail; a bad file fails at once.
Cancelling a running job is seen at the next heartbeat; the worker kills its ffmpeg and throws its half-made output away.
optimizations: Claims, heartbeats and results are single short statements; no database lock is held while a video converts.
Ad creatives have their own lane, so they never wait behind a film.
scale: A project runs at most 2 programme jobs at once across all servers, so one project's 500-video sync can't starve the others; the rest wait their turn.
Add servers to add workers (2 programme + 1 ad thread each, configurable); the table coordinates them.

Known limits: an interrupted conversion restarts from the beginning; an idle worker picks a new job up within about 2 seconds; two servers claiming at the same instant can put a project one job over its share.
Not measured: behaviour with many servers or thousands of queued jobs.
rules: Jobs belong to a project and are protected by row-level security like videos; another project's user gets 404.
Cancel needs the asset editing permission; with nothing queued or running the answer is 409 NOT_PROCESSING.
Finished jobs are kept for 30 days.
tests: MediaJobTest (10: duplicate enqueue, two workers, crash, stale worker, cancel queued and running, retries, permanent failure, fairness, isolation)

features.title: Connected video library: sync and prepare
features.summary: A project's existing video library (Mux today) is read into FAST Studio as a catalogue: every ready video appears as a Draft with its title and length, without fetching or converting anything. You then pick the videos you want on air and prepare only those. Syncs run in the background, continue where they stopped after an outage, never import a video twice and never overwrite what you edited here.
who: Platform administrators: connect the library, check the connection, start a sync (Connectors page)
Owners and content managers with the library-sync feature: start a sync and prepare videos (API; Library screen to follow)
Everyone in the project: see the library status

flow.title: Follow a library video from sync to air
flow.intro: The boxes are the parts involved; the pill is one sync or one video. Pick a situation.

nodes.label: Connection
nodes.sub: Encrypted keys, last check, sync checkpoint

nodes.label: Sync job
nodes.sub: Reads one page at a time

nodes.label: Catalogue
nodes.sub: Draft videos + where each came from

steps.say: A platform admin enters the library's access keys for a project.
They are stored encrypted. Saved keys alone don't count as a working connection.
steps.tech: AES-GCM ciphertext in `media_connection`; never returned by any API.

steps.say: "Check connection" reads the library with those keys.
The result and time are recorded, with the reason in plain words if it failed. New keys clear the old result.
Someone starts a sync. It runs in the background; a second click just shows the running one.
steps.tech: A SYNC row in `media_job`, at most one active per project.

steps.say: A worker reads the first page of the library.
The library answers with up to 100 videos.
Each ready video that is new becomes a Draft with its title and length. Videos still processing in the library wait for a later sync.
steps.tech: Unique on project + source, so nothing is imported twice.

steps.say: Before asking for the next page, the worker saves what it did and where to continue.
After the last page the sync is complete. Nothing was downloaded or converted.
Page 1 is done and saved; the worker asks for page 2.
The library doesn't answer.
The sync waits and tries again later (after 1, 5, 25 minutes…). Page 1 stays imported.
steps.tech: The job fails as retryable; the checkpoint still points at page 2.

steps.say: Next time it continues at page 2, without reading page 1 again.
The sync completes as if nothing happened.
You pick the Draft videos you want to air.
steps.tech: `POST /api/orgs/{org}/library/prepare` with up to 100 ids.

steps.say: Each video is checked on its own: from the library, still Draft, ready in the library, within the project's conversion limit.
Eligible videos are queued; the rest are listed with a reason (already ready, not ready in the library, limit reached…).
The preparation job fetches the video's original file from the library.
Converted into 5-second segments, the video is ready to schedule.
You give a synced video your own title and episode numbers.
Later, someone renames it in the library.
The next sync sees the new name.
Your title stays. What the library says is recorded next to it, not over it.
steps.tech: `asset_source` holds the library's title and status; the asset row is never touched by a re-sync.

steps.say: A video is deleted in the library.
A webhook flags it as deleted. If no webhook comes, the next complete sync flags it as missing.
The video and any media already prepared stay, so nothing scheduled breaks. Removing it is a separate, deliberate step.

steps: Platform administration → Connectors → a project → Mux video library: enter the access token ID and secret (and the webhook signing secret), then Check connection.
Sync library now: the page shows progress (videos seen, added as drafts, pages) and, after an outage, when it retries.
Projects with the library-sync feature can start the same sync with POST /api/orgs/{organization}/library/sync and watch it with GET /api/orgs/{organization}/library.
Prepare the videos you want to air: POST /api/orgs/{organization}/library/prepare with their ids. The answer lists anything that wasn't queued and why.
Your own direct uploads to the library still prepare automatically, because you uploaded them to air.
howItWorks: The connection (media_connection) stores the provider, encrypted keys, the last check and the sync checkpoint. Library code talks to the platform only through a provider adapter (IMediaProvider) that declares what the platform can do: CATALOGUE, DIRECT_UPLOAD, SOURCE_FILE, WEBHOOKS. Actions a platform can't do are refused with 409 NOT_SUPPORTED.

A sync is a durable SYNC job. The worker reads one page, imports it, then saves the next page's position under the job's fence; a crash, restart or outage continues from there. No database transaction or web request stays open while the library is called.

Importing a video is idempotent: a new ready video becomes a Draft asset bound by source_ref; a known one only updates its asset_source row (the library's title, length, status and when it was last seen).
When a full scan reaches its last page, videos of that library not seen since the scan started are flagged MISSING, in the same statement that completes the job.
Prepare marks each eligible video Processing and queues an ordinary packaging job, which fetches the original file and converts it.
Mux webhooks (created, ready, errored, deleted) take the same import path; a direct upload of ours is linked to its row and prepared at once.
optimizations: Pages of 100; one small insert or update per video and one checkpoint update per page.
Nothing is downloaded or converted during sync, so a large library costs only listing calls.
The connector switch is cached for 30 seconds, like the other connector checks.
scale: A sync runs on any server's media workers and counts as one of the project's 2 running jobs, so a huge library can't take every worker.
Only one sync per project can be queued or running; repeated clicks are free.

Known limits: one connection per project; if a server dies between importing a page and saving its checkpoint, that page is read again (nothing is duplicated, only the "videos seen" count goes up twice); the media-hours limit is checked once when a sync starts.
Not measured: libraries with tens of thousands of videos.
rules: Library videos arrive as movies (Draft). Nothing is prepared unless someone picks it, or it was our own direct upload.
Titles, episodes and rights edited in FAST Studio are never overwritten by a sync.
A video deleted or missing in the library is only flagged; its local copy and prepared media stay.
Prepare takes 1 to 100 videos and needs asset editing; starting a sync also needs the library-sync feature (platform administrators can always).
Project users never see the provider's name; credentials are write-only.
Not built yet: cancelling a running sync from the screen, choosing the media type per video at import, scheduled automatic syncs, the Library screen for picking videos.
tests: LibrarySyncTest (4: a catalogue-only fake platform, resume after an outage, edits kept and missing flagged, prepare selected)
MuxTest (connection check, catalogue-only sync, re-sync, white-label, signed webhooks incl. deleted)

features.title: Per-project limits
features.summary: Every project has a fair share: a cap on API requests per minute, on stored video hours and on videos converting at once, so one busy project can't slow everyone else down. Platform administrators set the limits per plan, tenant or project.
who: Every project is held to them

flow.title: See how a busy project is kept to its share
flow.intro: The boxes are the checks a request or a conversion passes; the pill is one request. Pick a situation.

nodes.label: Platform admin
nodes.sub: Sets limits per plan, tenant or project

steps.say: A platform admin sets "API requests per minute" for one tenant, or overrides it for one project.
The most specific value wins: project, then tenant, then the global default. 0 means unlimited.
steps.tech: Every server applies a change within a minute (cache lifetime).

steps.say: A script in one project calls the API very fast.
Requests are counted per project in one-minute windows.
Over the limit, the answer is "made more than N requests in a minute". It works again in the next minute.
Other projects keep their own allowance and notice nothing.
steps.tech: Known ceiling: counted per server, so N servers allow up to N times the limit.

steps.say: Someone uploads a video.
The project's stored hours (archived videos excluded) are compared with its limit first.
Refused with "already stores its limit of N hours". Archiving videos frees room.
Someone retries a failed video while many are converting.
The number of videos converting right now is compared with the limit.
Refused with "N videos are already converting"; try again when some finish.
A normal upload.
Within the requests per minute.
Within the stored hours.
The upload is accepted and its conversion is queued.

steps: Platform administration → Tenants → Manage <tenant>: under Custom properties, set "API requests per minute", "Stored media hours" or "Videos converting at the same time". Configuration scope "Tenant defaults" applies to all its projects; choose a project to override it for that project only.
Leave a value at the global default (6000 requests, 500 hours, 20 conversions), or use 0 for unlimited.
A project over a limit gets a clear message: "made more than N requests in a minute", "already stores its limit of N hours", or "N videos are already converting".
howItWorks: The limits are ordinary configuration properties (limits.api_requests_per_minute, limits.media_hours, limits.processing_videos): global default, then tenant value, then project override.
API requests are counted per project in one-minute windows as soon as the project of a request is known; over the limit the answer is 429.

Before an upload, a generated sample, a direct upload or a library sync, the project's stored hours (all videos except archived ones) are compared with its limit; before starting a conversion, the number of videos converting is compared with its limit; over either the answer is 409.
optimizations: Each project's limits are read at most once a minute per server (cached), so the check costs nothing on most requests.
Request counting is in memory: no database write per request.
Stored hours and conversions come from one query on an (org_id, status) index.
scale: Known ceiling: request counts are per server, so with N servers a project can make up to N times its limit. Upgrade path: Cloudflare rate limiting in front, or a shared counter.
The media-hours check runs once before a library sync, so one sync can go past the limit; the next one is refused.
Changing a limit takes up to a minute to apply on every server (cache lifetime).
rules: Limits are whole numbers; 0 means unlimited; anything else is refused (422).
Partner organizations are not counted (they have no content).
Videos arriving through library webhooks are not blocked by the conversion limit; fair scheduling of conversions is part of the durable job queue (Stage 2).

screenshots.caption: A tenant’s settings: the limits sit with its other properties (API requests per minute shown at its old default of 600, now 6000; stored media hours and conversions further down). "global" means the global default is in effect; Save override sets it for this tenant, or for one project when a project scope is chosen.

features.title: Tenant data export and deletion
features.summary: When a customer asks for its data or leaves, a platform administrator can export everything the tenant owns as one file, and then delete the tenant permanently, without touching any other customer.

flow.title: See what export and deletion touch
flow.intro: The boxes are the steps of an export or deletion; the pill is the request. Pick a situation.

nodes.label: Table catalog
nodes.sub: Finds every table with an organization

nodes.label: People
nodes.sub: Anonymized if only in this tenant

steps.say: A platform admin asks for the tenant's data.
The database catalog lists every table that carries an organization or tenant, so new tables are included automatically.
All rows of the tenant's projects are read.
One JSON file. Credentials, hashes, webhook secrets, ad-tag URLs and queued email text are left out. Video files are not included.
The tenant is suspended first; then the admin types its exact name to confirm.
Its channels are taken off air: open players switch to the standby slate.
Rows are deleted children-first in one transaction, so it either all happens or nothing does.
steps.tech: Order comes from the foreign keys.

steps.say: People who only belonged to this tenant are anonymized, not deleted, because audit records elsewhere may name them.
Other tenants are untouched; the action is recorded in the platform audit log.
steps.tech: Not yet: removing copies already on R2 edge storage.

steps.say: Someone tries to delete a tenant that is still active, or types the name wrong.
Refused: an active tenant can't be deleted, and a wrong name gets 400. Customers get 403 for both actions.
A consultant belongs to this tenant and another one.
Their account stays for the other tenant; only this tenant's memberships go.

steps: Export: call GET /api/platform/tenants/{tenant}/export (a platform personal access token works). The answer is a JSON file with the tenant, its projects, members and every table's rows.
Delete: first suspend the tenant (Platform administration → Tenants → Suspend).
Then call POST /api/platform/tenants/{tenant}/delete with {"confirm": "<the tenant's exact name>"}. The answer lists how many rows were deleted per table.
There is no screen for these two actions yet; they are API only.
howItWorks: The tables to export and delete are found from the database catalog: every table with an org_id, owner_org_id, partner_org_id or tenant_id column. New tables are covered without code changes.
Export leaves out credentials, hashes and unredacted mail (token ids and secrets, webhook secrets, ad-tag URLs, password and token hashes, queued email text).

Deletion runs in one transaction: channels are taken off the edge (a final ARCHIVED snapshot, so open players show the standby slate), references between the tenant's own tables are cleared, rows are deleted children-first using the foreign keys, projects and the tenant are removed.

People who belonged only to this tenant are anonymized (email, name and password replaced; sign-in tokens and personal tokens removed), not deleted, because audit records elsewhere may name them. People who also belong to another tenant keep their account.
Local video and upload folders of the deleted projects are removed; both actions are recorded in the platform audit log.
optimizations: One query per table, filtered by the tenant's organizations with = any(array), so each table is read or deleted with one index-assisted statement.
No hand-kept table list to fall out of date.
scale: Export builds the whole answer in memory: fine for a pilot tenant; for very large tenants (millions of playback events) stream it to a file instead. Not measured.
Deletion of a large tenant is one long transaction holding row locks only on that tenant's rows; other tenants are not blocked. Not measured at volume.
Known gaps: video copies already on the edge storage (R2) are not deleted yet, and there is no waiting period between deletion request and purge.
rules: Platform administrators only; customers get 403.
Deletion requires the tenant to be suspended and its exact name typed; otherwise 409 or 400.
Video files are not part of the export.
tests: TenantDataTest (export, then delete one tenant; the other stays untouched)
